query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing 1–2 at.% aluminum (Al) into equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr via modified melting processing will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 surface scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby significantly improving oxidation resistance without compromising the alloy’s room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength range of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Addition of 1–2 at.% aluminum during vacuum arc melting to modify the alloy’s surface chemistry.
generation.conditions: Exposure of alloy samples to atmospheric air at 800 °C for up to 5 hours under no mechanical load, ensuring that oxidation behavior is isolated from any stress effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy surface that acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum has a strong affinity for oxygen; when incorporated at low levels, it preferentially oxidizes at high temperatures to form a stable, slow-growing Al2O3 layer. This protective scale prevents rapid oxidation (pesting) while the bulk microstructure (and hence mechanical performance) remains intact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the Al-added variant is expected to show a significantly lower oxidation mass gain and more uniform, adherent oxide scale formation during a 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C, while preserving its room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and yield strength at 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: Original equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with rapid oxidation (pesting) issues under similar high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable under conditions where Al addition does not exceed ~2 at.% to avoid detrimental intermetallic phase formation. The test conditions are limited to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours with no applied load; outcomes outside these parameters (e.g., different temperatures or mechanical loading) are not evaluated.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the optimal Al content to balance oxidation resistance with phase stability; further investigation is necessary to confirm that minor Al additions do not adversely affect the alloy’s microstructure or mechanical properties across a broader range of temperatures and loading conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys—one set with an addition of 1–2 at.% Al and one untreated control. Subject both sets to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours under no applied load. Characterize the extent of oxidation (mass gain measurements, oxide scale morphology via SEM/EDS) and subsequently test room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength at 1000 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not exhibit a significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar mass gain and non-uniform scale formation as the untreated sample) or if its mechanical properties at room and high temperatures are degraded beyond acceptable limits relative to the control, the hypothesis will be rejected.
